newsitem.title: UK: Albright walks Churchill halls, declines his seat.
newsitem.headline: Albright walks Churchill halls, declines his seat.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright honoured the past and recalled her own history on Wednesday, touring the place where Winston Churchill led the war effort while she was a Czech refugee living in air raid shelters in London.
The main purpose of her stop was talks with British leaders on NATO expansion plans, alliance ties with Russia, Bosnia and the future of Hong Kong.
But Albright also used her visit to London as America's first female foreign minister to tour the fortified basement in Whitehall known as the cabinet war rooms.

It was there -- in a warren 10 feet (three metres) below ground -- that Prime Minister Churchill, his key cabinet minister, his chiefs of staff and his intelligence chiefs worked and slept from 1940 to 1945 as they plotted their moves during World War Two.
"This is very real to me," Albright told museum curator Philip Reed.

"I had a gas mask. I was in air raid shelters... Air raid sirens, blackouts. We sang a lot of boring songs and I ate an awful lot of cold meat and bubble and squeak," she said of her war years in London.

Exploring the cramped, primitive and dingy room where Churchill's cabinet held 115 meetings, Reed suggested Albright sit in Churchill's simple wooden chair at the head of the large table around which ministers gathered.
The secretary of state, known for her sense of history, declined, saying: "I think that's a little presumptuous."
Reminded that President Bill Clinton tested the chair in 1995, Albright replied: "Well, he's the president."

Albright, born 59 years ago to a diplomatic and academic family in Prague, fled Czechoslovakia with her family in 1939 and stayed in Britain through the war. They later returned to their home country but after the communist takeover in 1948, went to the United States.
"While they (Churchill and his cabinet) were sitting here, I was sitting in an air raid shelter in Notting Hill" in the cellar of a large apartment building, she said.
Later, when the family moved to Walton-on-Thames, she said they had a steel table, popular at the time as a survival device, under which family members would crowd during a bombing raid.

She could have never known then that this child of war would someday become the top diplomat for what she calls the world's "indispensable nation" with the opportunity to play a major role in shaping the post-Cold War peace.
An exponent of strong U.S. leadership and the use of force when necessary, Albright's views were shaped by her wartime experiences and the appeasement of Adolph Hitler at Munich.

A university professor of international relations earlier in her career, she showed a keen curiousity in the museum, asking questions, examining maps on the wall, reading original notes left on the work tables and putting her ear to a "scramble" telephone that was a critical link between British leaders and the world.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Albright had no plans to visit venues in London where she formerly lived as a child. Her background has been subject of much fascination since she was named secretary of state and became more so after disclosures her family was Jewish but converted to Catholicism in the 1930s as a defence against the Nazis.
London was the fifth stop on an 11-day, nine-country tour of Europe and Asia, Albright's first overseas trip since becoming secretary of state.
